Testing IIA and specification

Benjamin E. Bagozzi

Source: vignettes/iia.Rmd
iia.Rmd

The multinomial logit’s independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA) is a testable restriction, and the tests of it have a troubled history: the most cited one, in its classic form, often yields a covariance difference that is not positive semidefinite and a negative statistic, and implementations of the others differ in details that change the answer (which half of the sample is used, which weights, which covariance). polychoice implements the existing tests with their definitions fixed in the package’s design document, checks them by simulation, and reports what the simulation found. This vignette walks through the battery on the Pennsylvania vote data and then through the further specification tests.

library(polychoice)
data(pa2006)
m <- mnl(vote ~ canvass + phone + democrat + republican + age + female + voted2004,
         data = pa2006)

The IIA battery

Hausman and McFadden (1984)

Under IIA, dropping an alternative and refitting on the remaining cases leaves the common coefficients consistent, so the full-sample and restricted estimates should agree. The classic statistic uses the difference of the two covariance matrices, q=(β̂r−β̂f)′(Vr−Vf)−1(β̂r−β̂f)q = (\hat\beta_r - \hat\beta_f)'(V_r - V_f)^{-1}(\hat\beta_r - \hat\beta_f), which need not be positive semidefinite in finite samples; a negative statistic is reported with a p-value of 1 and a flag. The joint form estimates the covariance of β̂r−β̂f\hat\beta_r - \hat\beta_f from the stacked scores of the two fits (a seemingly-unrelated-estimation sandwich), which is always positive semidefinite. Dropping the base alternative re-bases the model exactly, so every alternative can be dropped.

hausman_mcfadden(m)
#> Hausman-McFadden test of IIA (variance difference) 
#>       alternative statistic df p.value   psd n_restricted
#>           abstain    -1.027 16       1 FALSE         1267
#>          democrat     1.586 16       1 FALSE         1419
#>  republican_other   -56.438 16       1 FALSE         1435
#>       nonresponse    -1.394 16       1 FALSE         1873
#> Note: psd = FALSE: the covariance difference is not positive semi-definite. A negative statistic is no evidence against IIA (p-value 1); a positive one is unreliable (the difference form over-rejects); use vcov = "joint".
hausman_mcfadden(m, vcov = "joint")
#> Hausman-McFadden test of IIA (joint (suest) covariance) 
#>       alternative statistic df p.value  psd n_restricted
#>           abstain    26.165 16  0.0517 TRUE         1267
#>          democrat    14.386 16  0.5700 TRUE         1419
#>  republican_other    11.353 16  0.7872 TRUE         1435
#>       nonresponse    11.398 16  0.7843 TRUE         1873

Small and Hsiao (1985)

The sample is split in half. The full model is fit on both halves and the two estimates are combined with the weights 1/2\sqrt{1/2} and 1−1/21 - \sqrt{1/2}; the model without the dropped alternative is fit on the second half; the statistic is minus twice the difference between the second-half restricted log-likelihood evaluated at the combined estimates and at its own maximum. It depends on the split, so splits repeats it over several random splits and seed makes the result reproducible.

small_hsiao(m, splits = 10, seed = 1)
#> Small-Hsiao test of IIA (stratified half-split, sqrt(1/2) weighting) 
#>  split      alternative statistic df  p.value separated
#>      1          abstain    61.525 16 2.89e-07      TRUE
#>      1         democrat    59.897 16 5.45e-07      TRUE

#>     10      nonresponse    25.730 16   0.0579     FALSE
#> 
#> Across splits:
#>       alternative median_statistic df median_p share_reject_05 share_separated
#>           abstain           22.987 16    0.114             0.5             0.5
#>          democrat           19.149 16    0.261             0.4             0.5
#>  republican_other           18.984 16    0.269             0.4             0.5
#>       nonresponse           14.004 16    0.598             0.1             0.0
#> separated = TRUE: a fit behind that row has diverging coefficients (quasi-separation in a half-sample); its statistic may reflect the separation rather than IIA.

The split matters, and on these data for a reason that has nothing to do with IIA. Only two of the 125 nonresponders did not vote in 2004. In four of the ten splits (1, 4, 5, and 10) both fall in the second half, so in the first half the nonresponse equation separates on voted2004 (its coefficient diverges); the combined estimate then gives those two respondents a near-zero probability in the second half, and the statistics of the three drops that keep nonresponse exceed 50 on 16 degrees of freedom, while the nonresponse drop, which removes that equation, stays below 26. The separated column marks every row whose statistic uses a diverging half-sample fit: the three drops that keep nonresponse in those four splits and in split 6 (where both fall in the first half; there the separated half carries the smaller weight and the evaluation half has neither case, so those statistics are small), but not the nonresponse drops, which remove the separated equation. In the five splits without separation only two of the 20 statistics reject at the 5 percent level, both in split 2. A single split can therefore suggest a decisive rejection or none, and which one is luck: on these data a split drawn with small_hsiao(m, seed = s) is separated for 12 of the seeds 1 to 20. The test is the split fixed before the data are seen (small_hsiao(m, seed = )): report it, and when it is separated, as split 1 is here, report it as uninformative or calibrate it by the parametric bootstrap with the same seed. A seed chosen after seeing a result is not a test. The splits and their summary (the median, the share of splits rejecting, and the share separated) describe how much the statistic varies; when many splits separate, the test has little to say about IIA on data like these. The summary’s median_p is the chi-square p-value of the median statistic, a descriptive figure: the median of several split statistics is not itself chi-square distributed (in the package’s size study a single split had nominal size, while the battery’s median rule never rejected under the null: it is conservative by construction). When the decision matters, calibrate the median by the parametric bootstrap: give boot_pvalue() a function that returns the median statistic as a one-row data frame, with a fixed seed so that every replicate draws its splits from the same random stream (they are stratified on each replicate’s simulated outcome; slow: ten splits refit the model thirty times per replicate, so this is not run here).

sh_median <- function(object, drop) {
  s <- attr(small_hsiao(object, drop = drop, splits = 10, seed = 1), "summary")
  data.frame(test = "Small-Hsiao median", statistic = s$median_statistic)
}
boot_pvalue(m, sh_median, B = 99, drop = "abstain")

Fok and Paap (2025)

Fok and Paap (2025) take the pairwise conditional likelihoods of the multinomial logit and build two tests: Q1Q_1, a Hausman contrast between the maximum-likelihood and the composite-likelihood estimates (the latter with a Godambe sandwich covariance), and Q2Q_2, a GMM overidentification test on the stacked pairwise scores. Q2Q_2 is computed in the two-step form by default (gmm = "iterated" and the projected C-statistic form are available); with the pairs that involve the base alternative only and case-specific covariates alone there is no overidentification and only Q1Q_1 is reported. Under the multinomial logit the composite-likelihood estimator is nearly as efficient as the maximum-likelihood one, so the difference of their two separately estimated covariance matrices, which Fok and Paap’s Q1Q_1 uses, is a small difference of noisy matrices and is indefinite in nearly every sample (the package’s simulations found 44 percent of these statistics negative). fp_tests() therefore estimates the covariance of the contrast directly from the two estimators’ stacked influence functions by default, as the joint Hausman-McFadden form does; vcov = "difference" gives Fok and Paap’s formula.

fp_tests(m)
#> Fok-Paap (2025) misspecification tests, all pairs 
#>                                            test statistic df p.value  psd pairs
#>                 Fok-Paap CL Hausman (Q1, joint)    42.692 24 0.01078 TRUE   all
#>  Fok-Paap GMM overidentification (Q2, two-step)    49.820 24 0.00149   NA   all

The battery

iia_tests() runs all of the above with one call, with ten Small-Hsiao splits reported by their median (the row’s p-value is the chi-square p-value of the median statistic, a descriptive figure).

iia_tests(m, seed = 1)
#> Tests of IIA / misspecification of the multinomial logit 
#>                                            test      alternative statistic df
#>                   Hausman-McFadden (difference)          abstain    -1.027 16
#>                   Hausman-McFadden (difference)         democrat     1.586 16
#>                   Hausman-McFadden (difference) republican_other   -56.438 16
#>                   Hausman-McFadden (difference)      nonresponse    -1.394 16
#>                        Hausman-McFadden (joint)          abstain    26.165 16
#>                        Hausman-McFadden (joint)         democrat    14.386 16
#>                        Hausman-McFadden (joint) republican_other    11.353 16
#>                        Hausman-McFadden (joint)      nonresponse    11.398 16
#>                Small-Hsiao (median over splits)          abstain    22.987 16
#>                Small-Hsiao (median over splits)         democrat    19.149 16
#>                Small-Hsiao (median over splits) republican_other    18.984 16
#>                Small-Hsiao (median over splits)      nonresponse    14.004 16
#>                 Fok-Paap CL Hausman (Q1, joint)                     42.692 24
#>  Fok-Paap GMM overidentification (Q2, two-step)                     49.820 24
#>  p.value   psd share_separated
#>  1.00000 FALSE              NA
#>  1.00000 FALSE              NA
#>  1.00000 FALSE              NA
#>  1.00000 FALSE              NA
#>  0.05174  TRUE              NA
#>  0.57001  TRUE              NA
#>  0.78718  TRUE              NA
#>  0.78430  TRUE              NA
#>  0.11408    NA             0.5
#>  0.26101    NA             0.5
#>  0.26950    NA             0.5
#>  0.59838    NA             0.0
#>  0.01078  TRUE              NA
#>  0.00149    NA              NA
#> psd = FALSE: the covariance difference was not positive semi-definite for that row. A negative statistic is no evidence against the model (p-value 1); a positive one from a variance-difference form is unreliable (see the test's help).
#> share_separated > 0: some Small-Hsiao splits had diverging half-sample fits; see small_hsiao(..., splits = ) for the split-level rows.
#> Small-Hsiao (median over splits): descriptive, not a test at its level (it rejected in none of 300 samples in the package's size study); for the test, run one split with its seed fixed in advance (small_hsiao(m, seed = ), or iia_tests(m, splits = 1, seed = )).

How to read this table for these data: the joint Hausman-McFadden rows do not reject at the 5 percent level (the abstention row only narrowly), and both Fok-Paap tests do. The Small-Hsiao medians are descriptive (the note under the table), and in three of their rows half the splits are separated. The difference-form Hausman-McFadden rows rest on covariance differences that are not positive semidefinite (psd = FALSE); one rule covers every such row: a negative statistic is no evidence against IIA (its p-value is 1), and a positive one is unreliable, because the difference form over-rejects (next section), so those rows are descriptive. The tests look at different departures, so disagreement is informative rather than contradictory: the Fok-Paap tests use all pairwise comparisons at once, while the drop tests look at one alternative at a time (and the Small-Hsiao medians here rest partly on separated splits). A reasonable report states the battery, notes which rows had an indefinite covariance difference, and, when the decision matters, calibrates the decisive statistic by the parametric bootstrap (next section) or fits the alternative model directly (nested logit, HEV, random intercepts; the Beyond IIA vignette) and compares by likelihood ratio.

What the size study found

The package’s verification ledger records a 300-replication study of the battery on data generated from the multinomial logit (three alternatives, four covariates, ten parameters, 1000 cases; Monte Carlo standard error about 0.013), with these rejection rates at the nominal 5 percent level: the Hausman-McFadden difference form was not positive semidefinite in 79 percent of replications and rejected 8 percent of the time for a non-base drop and 16 percent for the base drop; its joint form 2 and 5 percent; Small-Hsiao (one split) 4 and 5 percent, while the battery’s median over ten splits never rejected; Q1Q_1 in its joint form 6 percent; Q2Q_2 6 percent. Fok and Paap’s variance-difference form of Q1Q_1 rejected 4 percent of the time, but a separate 1,000-replication check of the same design showed that apparent calibration to be accidental: its covariance difference was never positive semidefinite, 44 percent of its statistics were negative, and it rejected 3.3, 4.2, and 4.9 percent of the time at the 1, 5, and 10 percent levels, while the joint form that fp_tests() uses by default rejected 1.5, 6.2, and 11.2 percent. An indefinite covariance difference can give a statistic of either sign: every form refers max⁡(statistic,0)\max(\text{statistic}, 0) to the chi-square, so a negative statistic has a p-value of 1. The practical recommendations that follow are:

  • read the difference form of Hausman-McFadden as descriptive and rely on its joint form, a single Small-Hsiao split with its seed fixed in advance (small_hsiao(m, seed = ); the median over several splits, which iia_tests() reports, is descriptive: in the size study it rejected in none of 300 samples), Q1Q_1 in its joint form, and Q2Q_2;
  • calibrate any of them with the parametric bootstrap when the decision matters (below);
  • remember that these are tests of IIA against unspecified alternatives; the score test against a nested logit (below) and the likelihood-ratio tests against the fitted nested logit, HEV, or random-intercept model (vignette Beyond IIA) are the sharper instruments when the alternative is known.

Parametric bootstrap calibration

boot_pvalue() takes a test function whose null hypothesis is the fitted model (the IIA tests, nested_lm_test(), captivity_test()) and returns a data frame with a statistic column, with its arguments, simulates B data sets from the fitted model, refits, recomputes the statistic, and reports the bootstrap p-value (1+k)/(B′+1)(1 + k) / (B' + 1), with B′B' the replicates that succeeded and kk the number of their statistics at least as large as the observed one, next to the asymptotic p-value. Replicates whose refit fails or loses an alternative are dropped and counted (n_failed); replicates whose refit raises a warning (diverging coefficients, a boundary, an ill-conditioned information matrix) are kept and counted (n_flagged, with the warnings tabulated in the attribute flag_reasons); the method line reports each count that is not zero. It is the remedy for a test whose finite-sample distribution is in doubt. Here it calibrates the two Fok-Paap tests, the rows of the battery that reject:

set.seed(2)
bf <- boot_pvalue(m, fp_tests, B = 399)
bf
#> Fok-Paap (2025) misspecification tests, all pairs -- parametric bootstrap, 399 replicates, 47 with a warning in the refit (attribute "flag_reasons"), up to 47 with an NA statistic left out of a row (attribute "n_na") 
#>                                            test statistic df p.value  psd pairs
#>                 Fok-Paap CL Hausman (Q1, joint)    42.692 24 0.01078 TRUE   all
#>  Fok-Paap GMM overidentification (Q2, two-step)    49.820 24 0.00149   NA   all
#>  p.boot
#>  0.0075
#>  0.0170
attr(bf, "flag_reasons")
#> The data are quasi-completely separated (see separation()) 
#>                                                         47
attr(bf, "p.boot_unflagged")
#> [1] 0.008498584 0.016997167

Calibrated, both Fok-Paap tests still reject. Two of the 399 replicate statistics reach the observed Q1Q_1, so its p.boot is 0.0075. The 47 flagged replicates are simulated samples in which the nonresponse equation separates on voted2004, the same mechanism as in the Small-Hsiao splits above: its intercept falls and its voted2004 coefficient rises without bound, their sum staying finite. Along that one direction neither estimator has an estimate, so Q1Q_1 leaves it out and compares the two estimators on the other 23, and Q2Q_2 is not computed in those samples (?fp_tests). Five of the other 352 replicate statistics reach the observed Q2Q_2, and its p.boot is 0.017. The observed data do not separate, and over the unflagged replicates the two p-values are 0.0085 and 0.017.

The score test against a nested logit

McFadden’s (1987) Lagrange-multiplier test asks whether the inclusive-value parameters of a specified nest structure differ from 1 (the multinomial logit) without fitting the nested model; nested_lm_test() computes it from the multinomial-logit scores (the outer-product information by default, the form of McFadden’s regression test). Here the nests group the two forms of non-participation against the two forms of voting.

nests <- list(out = c("abstain", "nonresponse"), vote = c("democrat", "republican_other"))
nested_lm_test(m, nests)
#> Lagrange-multiplier test of IIA against a nested logit 
#>                        test statistic df p.value
#>  Nested-logit LM test (opg)     2.299  2   0.317

Further specification tests

combine_test() asks whether two alternatives can be pooled (Cramer and Ridder 1991): the Wald form tests the equality of their slope coefficients (the constants stay free), the likelihood-ratio form compares the pooled fit with a binomial split term. term_test() tests every covariate jointly across equations (Wald or LR). hl_test() is the Hosmer-Lemeshow-type goodness-of-fit test for multinomial models of Fagerland, Hosmer, and Bofin (2008), with the observed and expected counts by decile of risk.

combine_test(m, c("democrat", "republican_other"))
#> Test of combining alternatives (Wald) 
#>                         pair statistic df p.value
#>  democrat & republican_other    318.28  7  <2e-16
term_test(m)
#> Joint tests of each term across equations (Wald) 
#>        term statistic df  p.value
#>     canvass     3.469  3  0.32486
#>       phone     0.557  3  0.90616
#>    democrat    98.148  3  < 2e-16
#>  republican   134.614  3  < 2e-16
#>         age    70.603  3 3.17e-15
#>      female    17.997  3  0.00044
#>   voted2004   129.610  3  < 2e-16
hl_test(m)
#> Fagerland-Hosmer-Bofin goodness-of-fit test (10 groups by the base alternative's fitted probability)
#>   statistic = 69.950 on 24 df, p = 2.22e-06
#>   1 expected count(s) below 5.

On these data the Hosmer-Lemeshow-type test rejects clearly: the fitted probabilities of the multinomial logit are miscalibrated in some deciles of risk, a sign of misspecification that the IIA tests above do not locate.

The IIA tests, the score test, combine_test(), and term_test() return data frames of class "iia_test" with a statistic column, so their results can be bound and filtered. boot_pvalue() calibrates those whose null is the fitted model; term_test() and combine_test() test a restriction of it and are refused (for a term, fit the model without it and use boot_lr_test()). hl_test() returns a list with the observed and expected tables, and iia_tests() a data frame of class "iia_battery".

References

Cramer, J.S. and Ridder, G. (1991). Pooling states in the multinomial logit model. Journal of Econometrics, 47, 267-272.

Fagerland, M.W., Hosmer, D.W. and Bofin, A.M. (2008). Multinomial goodness-of-fit tests for logistic regression models. Statistics in Medicine, 27, 4238-4253.

Fok, D. and Paap, R. (2025). New misspecification tests for multinomial logit models. Journal of Choice Modelling, 54, 100531. doi:10.1016/j.jocm.2024.100531.

Hausman, J.A. and McFadden, D. (1984). Specification tests for the multinomial logit model. Econometrica, 52, 1219-1240.

McFadden, D. (1987). Regression-based specification tests for the multinomial logit model. Journal of Econometrics, 34, 63-82.

Small, K.A. and Hsiao, C. (1985). Multinomial logit specification tests. International Economic Review, 26, 619-627.
